COURT REPORTER TRANSCRIPT PRICING CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What should this deposition invoice actually total?

Two calculators for the arithmetic every freelance court reporter and deposition stenographer does before sending an invoice: turn page count, turnaround speed, travel, copies, and exhibits into an invoice total and an effective hourly rate, and check whether an agency's flat per-page offer is worth the day once travel and production time are counted. Both run entirely in this browser.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Deposition transcript invoice

Enter the page count and per-page rate at minimum, then click Calculate invoice.

Invoice total

Line itemAmount

Copies the line items, the total, and the "arithmetic only" note as plain text to paste into an invoice or email.

Agency offer check

Many assignments come through an agency quoting one flat number instead of billing the client directly. This divides that offer by your total hours on the job so you can compare it to your own target hourly rate before accepting.

Enter the agency's offer and your total hours, then click Check this offer.

Agency offer result

What this does and doesn't do

Both calculators total the numbers you enter — page counts, rates, multipliers, fees, and hours. Neither one knows any court's official transcript-rate schedule, an agency's contracted rate, or which fees a specific bar or client will accept. Treat the output as the arithmetic behind your own invoice or acceptance decision, not a determination of what a client owes or what a contract requires.

Common questions

How do freelance court reporters price a deposition transcript?

Most freelance reporters bill a flat appearance fee for showing up, plus a per-page rate for the transcript itself. The per-page rate is usually multiplied for faster turnaround (expedited, daily, or same-day), and certified copies, exhibits, a rough draft, realtime feed, and travel are billed as separate line items on top.

How much more does expedited or daily turnaround cost?

There is no single industry-wide multiplier -- it varies by reporter, agency, and jurisdiction. This calculator starts with illustrative defaults (expedited about 1.5x the ordinary rate, daily about 2x, same-day or hourly about 3x) that you can edit to match your own rate card before it reaches the invoice total.

How do I check whether an agency's flat offer is worth taking?

Divide the agency's total pay (page count times its offered rate, plus any flat appearance fee) by your total hours on the job -- travel both ways, time at the appearance, and production time. That effective hourly rate is what the assignment actually pays, which a per-page headline rate alone does not show. The agency offer check on this page does that division and compares it to a target hourly rate you set.

Does this calculator know my state's official transcript-rate schedule?

No. It only multiplies the rates, page counts, and multipliers you enter -- it does not know any court's official transcript-rate schedule, any agency's contracted rate, or which fees a specific bar or client will accept. Check your own state's rules and any governing contract before invoicing.

Is this legal or financial advice?

No. This calculator only totals the numbers you enter -- it does not determine what a client owes, does not know your state's transcript-rate rules, and is not a substitute for reviewing your own rate card, contract, or a qualified professional's advice.

Weighing an offer and not sure whether the rate itself is any good? What is a good per-page rate for a court reporter? works through why the same $4.50 a page can pay $68 an hour on one deposition and $112 on another, and why a higher rate is not automatically the better job.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for checking your own rate card, state rules, and any governing contract. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (invoice_calculated, agency_offer_checked, summary_copied, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. Copying the summary puts it on your clipboard and nowhere else — the text is built in this browser and is never sent anywhere. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Pricing a mobile notary signing instead of a deposition transcript? The notary trip quote calculator prices travel, printing, waiting, and after-hours work the same way — nothing uploaded.

Also booking the sign language interpreter for the same deposition or hearing? The sign language interpreter rate calculator prices that assignment — hours, a booking minimum, travel, and an after-hours differential — nothing uploaded.

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet or a guess under a deadline — what a blank spreadsheet gives you and what it doesn't.

vs-spreadsheet-or-guessing.html.text:
← Court Reporter Transcript Pricing Calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet or a guess under a deadline

The arithmetic is the same either way: an appearance fee, a per-page rate multiplied for turnaround, certified copies, exhibits, a rough draft, realtime, and travel, added into an invoice total and divided by hours for an effective hourly rate. The difference is what happens when that arithmetic gets built from scratch, under a deadline, for a rush job or a second agency offer that just came in.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet or mental math can produce exactly the same invoice total as this calculator — the math is multiplication and addition, not anything exotic. What a blank spreadsheet or a phone screen does not give you is a place that already has every line a deposition invoice needs: appearance fee, per-page rate, the turnaround multiplier that applies to the transcript fee only and changes with the tier the client asked for (ordinary, expedited, daily, or same-day), certified copies, exhibits, a rough draft, a realtime uplift, and travel. Building that structure correctly once, on a deadline, and then building it again identically for the next job at a different turnaround tier, or for a second agency's offer, is where a dropped line or the wrong multiplier creeps in.

This calculator is that structure already built. Fill in the same fields for the invoice or the agency offer check and the same formula runs every time, so a rush job's price is not whatever felt about right in the moment. It also does the one division a per-page number alone never shows: an agency's flat offer divided by every hour the job actually costs, travel and production time included.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What should this deposition invoice actually total?This calculator's invoice result — free, private, no account.
Is an agency's flat per-page offer actually worth the day?This calculator's agency offer check, against your own target hourly rate.
My job has a billing rule this calculator doesn't model (a multi-day per-diem, a split co-counsel fee).A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any rule you can describe.
Does this match my state's official transcript-rate schedule or a governing contract?Neither. Check your own rate card, state rules, and any governing contract before invoicing.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't a spreadsheet just as accurate as this calculator?

A correctly built one is, because the arithmetic itself is multiplication and addition. The risk is not the math, it is building it correctly under a deadline — often between depositions on a phone — with no built-in reminder to apply the same turnaround multiplier to the transcript fee but not the appearance fee, or to price certified copies per page rather than per copy. A single dropped line changes the invoice total without showing an error.

When is a spreadsheet actually the better choice?

When the job has a billing rule this calculator does not model — a stepped per-diem for a multi-day deposition, a court's own official transcript-rate schedule that applies instead of a freelance rate card, or a split fee across co-counsel. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that is quick to fill in correctly and hard to get wrong by accident, for the common case of an appearance fee, a per-page rate, a turnaround multiplier, and the usual add-ons.

What does guessing miss that either a spreadsheet or this calculator would catch?

The turnaround multiplier compounding with page count, almost every time. It is easy to estimate a rush job's price in your head by nudging the ordinary rate up a bit, and much harder to also carry certified copies, exhibits, and travel through that same mental estimate without a place to write each one down. Both a spreadsheet and this calculator force every line onto the page on its own, which is what actually closes the gap between an invoice that looks about right and one that undercharges for the rush.

How do I tell whether an agency's flat per-page offer is actually worth the day?

Divide it by every hour the job really costs, not just the hours on the record. It is easy to judge a flat per-page offer against a mental sense of what transcripts usually pay, and much harder to also carry travel both ways, the appearance itself, and production time through that same estimate without writing the hours down. This calculator's agency offer check does that division as its own step, against a target hourly rate you set, which is what shows whether a per-page number that looks fine still pays a reasonable rate once the whole day is counted.

Does this replace checking my state's official transcript-rate schedule or a governing contract?

No, and it is not built to. This calculator and a spreadsheet both stop at the arithmetic: an invoice total and an effective hourly rate from the numbers you supply. Neither one knows any court's official transcript-rate schedule, an agency's contracted rate, or which fees a specific bar or client will accept — that still has to come from your own rate card, state rules, and any governing contract, checked before invoicing.

what-is-a-good-per-page-rate-for-a-court.text:
← Back to the court reporter transcript calculator

What is a good per-page rate for a court reporter?

It is the question every freelance reporter asks when an agency emails an offer, and it does not have an answer in the form it is asked. A per-page rate is a price per unit, and the units — pages, and the hours behind them — move from job to job. Two assignments at the same rate can pay wildly different amounts per hour of your life, and the rate itself gives you no way to tell which one you are looking at.

The same rate, twice, with opposite answers

Take an agency offering $4.50 a page plus a $75 appearance fee on a deposition you estimate at 120 pages. That is $615 either way. What decides whether it is a good day is the hours:

The jobTotal payYour hoursPer hour
Across town, straightforward, ordinary turnaround $6155.5$111.82
Two hours each way, a long waiting period, heavy exhibits $6159$68.33

Against an $85-an-hour target, the first job clears it comfortably and the second misses by $16.67 an hour — roughly $150 across the assignment. Nothing about the offer changed. Only the hours did, and the per-page rate cannot see them.

A higher rate is not automatically the better job

This is the part that catches people out, because it runs against the instinct that a bigger number is better. Compare the 120-page job above with a shorter one at a rate that looks stronger:

OfferTotal payYour hoursPer hour
120 pages @ $4.50 + $75 appearance$6155.5$111.82
60 pages @ $6.25 + $100 appearance$4755.5$86.36

The $6.25 rate is nearly 40% higher per page and pays $140 less in total, because a rate multiplies a page count and the page count halved. For the same 5.5 hours it returns $86.36 an hour against $111.82. It still clears an $85 target — by $1.36 — but a reporter who took it because the rate looked better gave up a quarter of the hourly return.

So what actually answers the question

One division, done before you accept rather than after you invoice:

(pages × per-page rate + appearance fee) ÷ every hour the job costs you = what it really pays

Then compare that against a target hourly rate you set once, from what you need the year to earn. The target is the figure worth deciding when you are not under deadline pressure; after that, every offer is a division and a comparison.

Count all the hours

  • Travel, both directions. The single biggest reason the two jobs above diverge.
  • On the record, plus waiting. Late starts and long breaks are hours whether or not anyone is speaking.
  • Production. Editing, proofreading, formatting, certifying. This is the block most often left out of a mental estimate, and it is the one a rush turnaround inflates.

That last point is why a turnaround multiplier is not free money. An expedited or daily tier raises the per-page rate precisely because it compresses production into fewer nights — so it belongs in the same division, with the extra hours counted, not treated as a bonus on top.

Do it on your own numbers

The court reporter transcript calculator on this site does both halves of this free and in your browser. The agency offer check takes a page count, the agency's rate and appearance fee, your total hours and your target hourly rate, and tells you the effective hourly rate and the shortfall — the arithmetic behind every figure on this page. The invoice calculator goes the other way for work you are billing yourself: appearance fee, travel, per-page rate with an editable turnaround multiplier, certified copies, exhibits, rough draft and realtime, totalled into an invoice and a plain-text summary you can paste into an email.

Nothing you type is uploaded, there is no account, and it costs nothing.

Common questions

Can a per-page rate on its own tell me whether a job is worth taking?

No, and that is the whole difficulty. A per-page rate multiplies a page count you cannot know in advance and says nothing about the hours the job will cost you. The same offer of $4.50 a page plus a $75 appearance fee on a 120-page deposition pays $615 either way — but spread over 9 hours of travel, appearance and production that is $68.33 an hour, and over 5.5 hours it is $111.82 an hour. One of those clears an $85 target and the other misses it by $16.67, from an identical headline rate.

Why can a higher per-page rate pay less than a lower one?

Because the page count moves too, and the page count is what the rate multiplies. A 60-page job at $6.25 a page with a $100 appearance fee totals $475 — $140 less than the 120-page job at $4.50 that totals $615. If both cost you 5.5 hours, the smaller job pays $86.36 an hour against the larger one's $111.82. The higher rate is the worse deal here despite looking better on paper, because a rate is a price per unit and the units are not fixed.

Which hours should I count when working out an effective hourly rate?

All of them, or the figure flatters the job. Count travel in both directions, the time you are actually on the record plus any waiting, and production time — editing, proofreading, formatting and certifying the transcript, which on a rush turnaround is the part that grows. Production is the hour block most often left out of a mental estimate, and it is the one that decides whether an expedited multiplier is compensation for extra work or just a bigger number next to a longer night.
